“#Prevent, #Engage and#Act”

These were the three keywords I brought back home from the ReAct Asia Pacific Regional Conference on#AMR 2026, held in Jakarta last week.
 
Just ahead of#WAAW2026, clinicians, researchers, policymakers, CSOs and youth came together for two days to deliberate on a collective course of action for the years ahead.

#Prevent: The updated WHO Global Action Plan (2026–2036) puts prevention first. As one speaker put it, infection control, immunisation and WASH are among the most powerful AMR programmes we have. That means stopping infections before they need #antibiotics. Another session suggested teaching infection prevention to students early, so they carry it into practice and pass it on to their peers.

#Engage: AMR can’t be fixed by the health sector alone. One participant asked where the ministers of agriculture and environment were in the room, and another said the finance minister should be involved from day zero. The session that stayed with me most put people at the centre. AMR survivor Ankita Mitra reminded us that an infection may be diagnosed in one person, but the consequences are lived by an entire family. Civil society, communities, and young people have to be part of the solution.

#Act: Plans are only as good as their delivery. Most plans are not costed, and WHO shared that only about 10% of countries had domestic funding for their national action plans in 2024. The call from the room was to cost the plan, set measurable indicators, close the reporting gap, and scale what already works.

My biggest learning was seemingly obvious: AMR cannot be tackled without addressing the systemic challenges that sit beneath it. Plans stay unfunded, sectors stay siloed, and accountability stays weak. Access to antibiotics and diagnostics remains unequal, and infection control and primary care are still stretched thin. Climate change, disasters and conflict make all of this worse, because every flood or crisis can become an AMR event.
 
Underneath all of it is social inequity. Those who are poorer, more displaced, and further from care are the ones who face the weakest infection control, the limited access to diagnostics, and the highest costs when treatment fails. That is why so many well-designed plans don’t deliver: they work best for those who already have access. AMR is not only a health problem. It is a development problem and a health-system problem, and it needs to be treated as both.

We enountered some of these stories through the #SochSamajhKe fellowship, whichSuperheroes Against Superbugs organized earlier this year in collabortion withYouth Ki Awaaz. Seeing them echoed in Jakarta was a strong motivation for us to continue our work at SaS.

Can Computer Vision turn water segmentation into a river flood alert system?
I  m Introducing RiverWatch — a video-based river monitoring system built around semantic segmentation and temporal water-area analysis.
I fine-tuned aSegFormer-B2 model to segment water surfaces in video footage, achieving a validation Dice score of0.92, with a validation Dice loss of 0.0344 at epoch 19/20.
But segmentation was only the first step.
RiverWatch measures the area held by the water mask in each sampled frame, compares it against an initial baseline, and evaluates the percentage increase to trigger four alert levels:
LOW · MEDIUM · HIGH · CRITICAL
The system combines:
SegFormer-B2: Fine-tuned semantic segmentation for water-surface identification.
Water-area monitoring: Quantifies segmented water coverage in pixels across sampled frames.
Baseline-based anomaly detection: Evaluates water-area growth against initial normal measurements.
Flood alert engine: Converts measured changes into graded risk alerts.
Interactive dashboard: Visualizes water masks, area measurements, alert levels, and temporal trends.
The model training involved multiple datasets, a multi-stage fine-tuning strategy, and domain adaptation using Andean river footage.
The application integrates a FastAPI backend and a React dashboard, with video processing and segmentation-based monitoring.
I deliberately simplified the original Computer Vision approach by removing the computationally expensive optical-flow pipeline and focusing on water-mask area monitoring, a measurable signal that can be tracked over time.
The objective: turn visual segmentation into an interpretable river-monitoring mechanism.
RiverWatch is an experimental community-oriented flood-monitoring prototype, not a validated flood forecasting system. Camera stability, segmentation quality, and environmental conditions remain critical limitations.
I trained it  from RIWA  Dataset from Kaggle and the Parepare semantic dataset from Indonesia monsoon flooding so this model can detect muddy water bodies as clear blue water lake and rivers as well water area region.
Stack: SegFormer · PyTorch · Hugging Face Transformers · OpenCV · FastAPI · React · TypeScript · Tailwind CSS · Docker.

Sarsha Braim read her job offer on a bathroom break, halfway through a waitressing shift.

Last month she was in Cannes for MIPCOM (her first time in France), selling sport content to TV broadcasters alongside studios like Paramount and Disney.

Not long before that offer, she'd finished uni, applied for a few jobs in sport and heard nothing back. She had about 10 LinkedIn connections, all from one uni class, and was convinced that "I'm not some big CEO, so no one wants to hear from me."

55 days after joining TheSportsGrad Method, she was approached for a job at Inverleigh, a sports media company she'd never heard of.

So what did she do differently?

She started posting about ice hockey, a sport she genuinely loves and that hardly anyone in Australia was writing about. Then every time someone liked or reacted to a post, she sent them a connection request within 24 hours, "while it's still fresh," so they'd remember her name.

One of those people was a co-founder of Inverleigh. He passed her name on to the company's commercial director, and the director messaged her about a job.

Posting on LinkedIn gets you seen, but the job comes from what you do after someone notices you. Think of a like as a wave from across the street: you can wave back and keep walking, or you can cross the road and say hello.

Today Sarsha is Commercial Partnerships Manager, Asia Pacific, flying to Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia to sell sport content to broadcasters.

If you want to try it this week:
1. Pick a sport you could post about for months (bonus points if hardly anyone else is covering it).
2. Post one thing you've noticed about it through the lens of the job you want. Partnerships? Break down a club's sponsors. Events? Review a match day. Analytics? Unpack one stat.
3. Set a 24-hour rule: everyone who reacts gets a connection request with a short note about the post.

Devo, I know, most of your posts will get a handful of likes and plenty of people won't accept. But you're not waiting on a job ad anymore, and you only need the right person to remember you.

Congrats Sarsha!!

Chinese technology companies are facing fresh disruption to their overseas #AI computing plans as Washington moves to close a route that has allowed them to access advanced U.S. chips through data centers in#SoutheastAsia.

New rules from the U.S. Commerce Department require export licenses for advanced chips and servers shipped to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. They also cap the computing power those facilities can provide to Chinese customers, threatening arrangements used by tech giants including #ByteDance, #Alibaba and#Tencent.

For companies that have relied on cloud capacity in Southeast Asia to train large AI models, the impact could be immediate. 

The restrictions also add to the pressure from the resignation of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who had been one of the industry's most prominent voices opposing Washington’s tighter chip controls.

Domestic suppliers such as Huawei could benefit as Chinese developers accelerate efforts to build models using homegrown processors. But the gap between domestic chips and Nvidia’s most advanced products remains a major obstacle.

Still reflecting on an energising two days in Singapore Million Cool Roofs Collective Co-Create Convening on the 18th and 19th of Nov.   

Grateful to have been in the room thanks to a timely invitation fromSitti Azzahra andYuh Ching Ang atArup forSustainable Living Lab (SL2) Group to partner up as Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) and community engagement partners for the Indonesian market. And of course to Pak Mahdi fromRuma.id who is part of our team as a progressive developer willing to help test our hypothesis at his properties!

Stepping into this space alongside 100+ participants from 65+ organisations across Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand made it clear just how critical this moment is for urban cooling in Southeast Asia.   

Beyond the buzz in the room, a few key takeaways stood out on what it actually takes to scale passive cooling:
1. Evidence gap is the real bottleneck: Solution providers already have proven cool roof products ready to deploy, yet many lack accessible local testbeds to generate the empirical performance data needed to unlock wider adoption.
2. Systems change requires a holistic play: Rather than focusing on technology in isolation, MCRC is designed to tackle the ecosystem from all angles, strengthening supply, stimulating demand, and building that critical local evidence base to influence policy and earn market trust.
3. Radical collaboration beats working in silos: Moving from a cool roof to 'Challenge' to a cool roof 'Collective' is truly the stand for me. Watching teams across all three countries openly share ideas, give candid feedback, and actively build on each other’s projects, was so refreshing. 

The energy across both days was top-notch, and huge credit goes to the MCRC team atSecondMuse, Clean Cooling Collaborative, and the local partners: Instellar Impact, Biji-biji Initiative, and PXP Sustainability, for organising such an intentional convening. I especially appreciated how sessions like Points of Connection, the Idea Gallery, and Cross Border Exchange were curated to constantly rotate us across tables and spaces with new teams. That structure made networking effortless and allowed us to genuinely learn about each other's ideas and on-ground capabilities.   

Excited to carry this momentum into the Prove phase and get the ball rolling toward real heat resilience across Southeast Asia!

300,000+ people in shelters: Cyclone Akvan has crossed India's east coast near Gopalpur in Odisha, weaker than feared but bringing very heavy rain 🌀

Akvan weakened from a severe cyclonic storm to a cyclonic storm overnight and crossed the south Odisha and north Andhra Pradesh coast close to Gopalpur between 07:30 and 08:30 on Friday morning India time, with winds of 70-80 km/h gusting to 90 km/h, the India Meteorological Department said (Deccan Chronicle, All India Radio). Odisha officials say more than 3 lakh (300,000) people have been moved to safer places, 423 rescue teams are deployed, 9,341 cyclone shelters are open, 69 trains are cancelled and schools are closed in 15 districts (The Hindu, All India Radio).

Why it matters: cooler coastal water and drier air took some of the storm's strength, which lowers the risk of wide damage to homes and power lines, but rain remains the main danger (India Today). Patrapur in Ganjam district recorded 209 mm in 24 hours and Gopalpur about 190 mm (Sambad English). The IMD warned of a storm surge in low-lying parts of Ganjam and Puri, and a red alert is in place for Srikakulam and Vizianagaram in Andhra Pradesh. Akvan is the third cyclone to threaten this coast in under a month, after Arnab and Murasu, and is expected to weaken into a depression over Odisha later today.

*“Coating reliability begins with technical details that must never be overlooked, both in documented procedures and during actual field application.”*

📍 Batam, Indonesia | 18–20 November 2026

During a recent Pre-Qualification Test (PQT), I had the opportunity to supervise two critical inspection tests that are sometimes overlooked by vendors, both during coating procedure preparation and actual surface preparation and painting application: the MEK Rub Test for Inorganic Zinc (IOZ) primers on Carbon Steel and the Ferroxyl Test for free iron contamination on Stainless Steel.

Although these tests address different technical risks, both play an important role in preventing premature coating failure and corrosion.

For Carbon Steel, the MEK Rub Test, in accordance with ASTM D4752, evaluates the degree of curing of Ethyl Silicate IOZ primers. The test involves rubbing the coated surface with an MEK-saturated cotton cloth for 50 double rubs, approximately one second per double rub. Results are rated from 0 to 5, with Rating 5 indicating the highest solvent resistance. Acceptance criteria shall follow the project specification and coating manufacturer's recommendations. Without this verification, insufficient curing may remain undetected, potentially resulting in poor intercoat adhesion, delamination, and premature coating failure.

Meanwhile, for Stainless Steel, the Ferroxyl Test, referenced in ASTM A380/A380M, detects free iron contamination introduced during fabrication, grinding, or contact with carbon steel equipment. The test involves applying a freshly prepared solution containing potassium ferricyanide, nitric acid, and distilled water to the surface. Blue staining, typically appearing within approximately 15 seconds, indicates detectable free iron contamination. The acceptance criterion is no blue staining within the specified observation period, followed by thorough rinsing. Without this inspection, contamination may remain undetected, potentially leading to rust staining, localized corrosion, reduced corrosion resistance, and costly rework.

These experiences remind us that coating quality goes beyond surface profile, environmental conditions, DFT, and visual inspection. As coating engineers and inspectors, our responsibility is to ensure that every applicable critical inspection requirement is clearly documented, technically understood, and properly implemented, from vendor procedure reviews and PQT through actual production.

A successful PQT is not simply about passing the tests performed, but ensuring that no critical inspection requirement has been overlooked.

*Sometimes, preventing a major coating failure starts with a small inspection that others might overlook.*

posts.text:
Hiring from Indonesia? Here is the legal pathway, step by step.

Getting the order of the paperwork right saves weeks. This is how a compliant placement runs:

1. Job order. You issue a demand letter and employment contract: role, salary, hours, accommodation, contract length.

2. Embassy endorsement. The job order is verified by the Indonesian Embassy or Consulate in your country.

3. Licensed recruiter. A licensed Indonesian placement company (P3MI) registers the job order and runs recruitment. Only licensed P3MIs can place workers abroad.

4. Selection and training. Candidates are screened, trained and certified for the role, with language preparation for your country.

5. Pre-departure. Medical check, social security (BPJS Ketenagakerjaan), visa and work permit, and a pre-departure orientation before the flight.

Where TalentXID fits: we source and train candidates through our LPK network and school partners, and work with licensed P3MI partners on verified job orders. After arrival, we stay in touch with workers to support retention.

Planning 2027 hires in hospitality, healthcare, welding or maritime? Start with step 1. Message us and we will check your job order requirements.

Here is the line most people will scroll past in the Mistral AI announcement: some of its earliest model customisation projects anywhere in the world were with Singapore's defence and homeland security agencies.

That reframes the whole story. Mistral did not come to Singapore chasing the AI hype. It followed a customer that was already paying attention.

Every big AI lab now has a Singapore story. OpenAI picked the city-state for its first Applied AI Lab outside the US. Anthropic opened an office here last month. Mistral has gone further, naming Singapore its Asia-Pacific HQ and pledging to more than double regional headcount to 200 by 2027. With 900-plus staff worldwide, Asia Pacific could become as much as a fifth of the company.

The numbers say commitment. What I see is a familiar match: a neutral city meeting a neutral vendor.

Singapore has spent decades selling itself as the place both sides can trust. It hosted the 2018 Trump-Kim summit and houses regional teams for American and Chinese tech giants alike. Mistral is selling the same thing in model form: open weights you can run on your own servers, neither American nor Chinese, and a European pedigree a minister can explain to voters.

But the region has seen this playbook before. Plenty of tech companies have planted a flag in Singapore, cut the ribbon, and then served Jakarta, Bangkok and Hanoi through a sales team and a slide deck. The HQ became a showroom.

Sovereign AI makes that harder to get away with. A government that wants control over its models will also want to know where its vendor's engineers sit. And 200 people in one city-state is a long way from a real presence in ten markets.

Then there is hiring. Mistral needs 100-plus specialists from the same small pond that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Databricks are already fishing in. 🎣

So, a question for my network: will Southeast Asia's sovereign AI be built from Singapore, or merely sold from there?

posts.text:
Andrew Fox gets the diagnosis right. China isn't dumping. It is exporting the consequences of involution: domestic overcapacity so severe that margin-seeking abroad has become operational necessity, not strategy. The West isn't losing because it is being cheated. It is losing because it optimised for a game China stopped playing.

But the framing is bilateral. Two models. Two scorecards. Who adapts wins.

That erases 150 countries.
If you sit in Riyadh, Nairobi, Jakarta, or Brasilia, the question is not which model is more rational. It is which form of dependency you are being offered, and whether either builds anything where you are.

The Western model sells margin. High prices, IP lock-in, platform rent, consulting layers that never transfer capability. Capital efficiency compounds upward for the seller. You pay the premium indefinitely. The Chinese model sells volume. Cheap goods, supply chain capture, infrastructure financing on terms that look generous until you examine the dependency they create. Scale compounds for the exporter. Your own industrial base never forms. Neither model builds capacity in the receiving nation. One extracts through price. The other displaces through volume. The sovereignty outcome is identical: permanent dependency on an industrial base you do not control.

Fox lists where scale-over-return logic applies. Solar. Batteries. EVs. Then, in passing: now AI. He moves on.

He should not have moved on.
When China applies involution logic to physical goods, what arrives is a car or a panel. The supply chain sits elsewhere, but the product is inert. When the same logic applies to AI, what arrives is not a product. It is inference infrastructure that embeds itself in how governments decide, how enterprises allocate capital, how citizens access services. Singapore's national AI programme dropped Meta's Llama and rebuilt on Alibaba's Qwen. African developers are building language models on DeepSeek and Qwen because the weights are accessible, affordable, and inspectable. Xi Jinping pledged 5,000 AI training slots for developing countries at the 2026 World AI Conference.

This is not margin-seeking. It is architectural. And it is happening while the bilateral debate about who is cheating whom absorbs all the oxygen.

The question that matters is not which incentive model is more rational. It is who is building, and where. For most of the world, the answer remains: not here.
